 2 Safe S&P 500 Financial Dividend Stocks Boomers Can Buy and Hold Forever
 By Lee Jackson 
 Published November 16, 2026, 7:49am ET · 5 min read 
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 JPMorgan and BlackRock pair rising dividends with huge earnings, yielding about 2% each, making them anchors for retirees seeking growing income.
 JPMorgan's dividend consumes only about 26% of earnings, backed by a 14% CET1 ratio, despite its 2009 cut from $0.38 to $0.05.
 BlackRock held its dividend steady through 2008 and 2009 while banks slashed payouts, and its fee-based model carries no loan book risk.

 Anyone who owned bank stocks through 2008 recalls how a dividend cut feels. JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE:JPM | JPM Price Prediction ) cut its quarterly payout from $0.38 to $0.05 in 2009, and much of the financial sector did the same. Since then, a small group of financial giants has built bigger capital cushions, steadier fee income and dividend records that keep rising. JPMorgan and BlackRock ( NYSE:BLK ) are two of the best examples. Both pay modest yields. For a retiree, the appeal is a growing income stream backed by very large earnings, and the risks are spelled out below for each company.
 JPMorgan Chase: Fortress Capital Behind a Rising Payout
 JPMorgan is an S&P 500 member with an index weight of about 1.34% and a market value of roughly $919.35B. It runs a consumer bank, an investment bank and a wealth manager under one roof. That mix holds up over time. In the third quarter, the bank kept the number one position in retail deposit share [ 1 ] based on FDIC data. It added about 650,000 [ 1 ] net new checking accounts, and its asset and wealth arm manages $5.2 trillion in assets under management. When one business slows, the others usually help make up the difference.

 Current yield: At a recent price of $346.19, JPMorgan yields 1.79%. Shareholders received $6.15 per share over the trailing 12 months. The latest quarterly dividend rose to $1.65 from $1.50, which puts the annualized forward rate at $6.60.
 How Safe Is JPMorgan’s Dividend?
 Free cash flow tells you little about a bank, because deposits and loans pass through its cash flow statement. The right measures are earnings coverage and regulatory capital . On earnings, trailing diluted EPS of $23.84 compares with $6.15 in trailing dividends, so the dividend uses only about 25.8% of earnings. Third-quarter net income was $15.3 billion [ 1 ] , with EPS of $5.57 and a return on tangible common equity of 20%.
 On capital, the standardized CET1 ratio stood at 13.9% [ 1 ] after the third quarter. The bank’s first-quarter filing reported $291B [ 2 ] of CET1 capital, $572B of total loss-absorbing capacity and $1.5T in cash and marketable securities. Jamie Dimon estimated "probably $30 billion or something of excess capital" [ 1 ] and was clear about where the dividend ranks: "After you pay your dividend, which hopefully will be steady, we really like investing in organic growth."
 A Track Record That Includes the 2009 Cut
 The payout fell to $0.05 in 2009 and stayed there through 2010. It recovered to $0.25 in 2011 and has risen since, reaching $0.90 in 2020 (held flat that year), $1 in 2022 and $1.65 today. The records show no reduction since the rebuild began. The biggest change since 2008 is the size of the capital and liquidity cushion. The core business has stayed the same: JPMorgan lends money, and losses rise when borrowers struggle. The credit card net charge-off rate is 3.33%, and the bank holds a $31.4B allowance for credit losses.
 Why It Fits a Decades-Long Hold
 JPMorgan trades at about 15 times trailing earnings and 14 times forward earnings. Its share price is up 466.11% over 10 years. With the dividend using only about a quarter of earnings, there is room for increases to keep outpacing inflation. Buybacks also reduce the share count over time. A new $50B [ 3 ] repurchase program took effect this year.
 What would break the case: a deep recession that forces a long rate-hiking cycle. CFO Jeremy Barnum put it plainly: "If the central bank needs things to cool off and that involves an aggressive, extended rate cycle, almost by definition that is going to involve higher unemployment, which will produce weaker consumer credit results." [ 1 ] If credit losses rise enough to eat into capital and regulators limit payouts, as they did in 2009, the dividend thesis would need a fresh look.
 BlackRock: Fee Income From a $15 Trillion Platform
 BlackRock, an S&P 500 component, manages a record $15.49T in client assets. It runs the iShares ETF family and the Aladdin risk and portfolio technology platform. Through Global Infrastructure Partners, HPS Investment Partners and Preqin, it has also expanded into private markets and data. BlackRock earns fees on the money it manages instead of lending its own balance sheet, so it carries no loan book that can go bad. Clients added $205B [ 4 ] in third-quarter net inflows, and management said inflows came from "every asset class, every client type, every region" [ 5 ] .
 Current yield: At $1,222.91, BlackRock yields 1.84%. Trailing 12-month dividends total $22.40 per share. The quarterly payout of $5.73 reflects a 10% raise, which puts the annualized forward rate at $22.92.
 How Safe Is BlackRock’s Dividend?
 For a fee-based asset manager, the right tests are earnings coverage and operating margin , because steady fees on a huge asset base are what fund the dividend. Trailing diluted EPS of $43.92 against $22.40 in dividends means the payout uses about 51% of GAAP earnings. That leaves a comfortable margin. Third-quarter adjusted EPS was $15.93 [ 4 ] , beating the $14.24 estimate, and the adjusted operating margin reached 47.8%. Planned buybacks for the year rose to roughly $2.0B. CFO Martin Small described the order of priorities: "We invest first in the business and then return excess cash to shareholders through a combination of dividends and share repurchases." [ 5 ] 
 No Cut Through the Financial Crisis
 BlackRock’s regular quarterly dividend has risen from $0.20 in 2003 to $5.73 today. Through 2008 and 2009, when banks were slashing payouts, BlackRock held its dividend at $0.78. It then raised it to $1 in 2010. The records show no reduction in the regular quarterly amount over that entire stretch, and recent increases run from $4.13 in 2021 to the current level.
 Why It Fits a Decades-Long Hold
 Organic base fee growth hit 11% [ 5 ] , the ninth consecutive quarter at or above 5%. Retirement savings, ETF adoption and private credit demand all feed the same platform. President Robert Kapito noted that "fixed-income demand remains in the early innings," [ 5 ] and that trend benefits BlackRock’s bond ETFs directly. Its shares trade at about 28 times trailing earnings and 19 times forward earnings, a premium for a business with this record. The stock is up 320.43% over 10 years.
 What would break the case: a long bear market. BlackRock’s fees rise and fall with market levels, so a prolonged downturn would reduce assets and revenue together. With a beta of 1.382, the stock tends to swing more than the overall market. If the GIP, HPS and Preqin deals fail to deliver the steadier private-markets fees management expects, dividend growth could slow to a crawl.
 Two Financial Pillars for a Lifetime of Income
 JPMorgan brings capital strength, with a dividend using about a quarter of its earnings and a CET1 ratio of 13.9% [ 1 ] . BlackRock brings fee income that kept its dividend intact through 2008 and 2009. One makes from lending and deposits, the other from managing trillions in client assets, so they lean on different drivers. Together they give a long-term income portfolio two growing dividends, each with large earnings and capital behind it (we rated ten more buy-and-hold dividend giants by valuation in a free Dividend Kings report here: 10 Dividend Kings to Buy Now and Hold Forever ).
